capture.final_message:
Use the principal-branch representation
\[
f(z)^{g(z)}=\exp\!\bigl(g(z)\,\Log(f(z))\bigr).
\]

The hypothesis \(f(x)\in\mathbb C.\mathrm{slitPlane}\) is essential: the principal logarithm is analytic there. Since the slit plane is open and analytic maps are continuous, \(f\) maps some neighborhood of \(x\) into the slit plane (or, in the relative case, does so eventually within \(s\)).

Organize each proof by:

1. Establishing that \(\Log\circ f\) is analytic at \(x\), respectively analytic within \(s\) at \(x\), using \(f(x)\in\mathrm{slitPlane}\).
2. Combining this with analyticity of \(g\) to obtain analyticity of \(z\mapsto g(z)\Log(f(z))\).
3. Composing with the entire function \(\exp\), then identifying the result with the complex power \(f(z)^{g(z)}\).

The two conjuncts follow from the same argument, using the ordinary and “within” versions of the analytic composition lemmas.
